newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Marines evacuate Americans fleeing Sierra Leone coup.
newsitem.headline: Marines evacuate Americans fleeing Sierra Leone coup.

text.p: U.S. marines using 15 helicopters evacuated Americans and others fleeing violence in Sierra Leone on Friday despite orders by coup leaders closing the country's airspace.
Military and diplomatic sources said rebel commanders had joined leaders the coup leaders and were rejecting any mediation to try and reverse the overthrow of the elected government.

The first four C-46 Sea Knight helicopters flew from the U.S. warship Kearsarge 12 miles off Freetown and landed by a city hotel where Americans had been assembling since daybreak. Scores of marines backed by fast-attack vehicles joined Nigerian troops already in position to secure the hotel.

"It began about 4 a.m. EDT (0800 GMT) and it is going very fast," said Pentagon spokeswoman Nancy Burt. She said 92 evacuees had been carried out on three helicopter missions so far -- 57 Americans and 35 from various other countries.
The marines were also taking out the last four of 26 members of the U.N. refugee organisation who had been based in the country, the UNHCR said in Geneva.
There was no sign of the Sierra Leone military, whose leaders ousted the elected government of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah last Sunday prompting an international outcry.
Regional power Nigeria has built up a force in Freetown over the past week and is expected to move against coup leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah under a regional mandate.

Diplomats said the closure of land, sea and air borders, announced by the Freetown Authorities on Thursday night, was to stop the Nigerian buildup. Sierra Leonean sources said it was also an attempt to impede the departure of Westerners to minimise chances of military action.

The military and diplomatic sources said leaders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), who had been waging a guerrilla campaign since 1991 but were now welcomed as allies by the coupmakers, entered the capital two days ago.

"The RUF leaders came out of the bush and entered the town. Now it seems the soldiers have got more than they bargained for because the rebels are now calling the shots," a West African peacekeeping officer said.
A diplomat involved with attempts to strike a deal with Koromah said a veteran politician sent to mediation talks at military headquarters on Thursday night found 50 rebel commanders there.
"They were sitting with the coup leaders, who had their military ranks stripped from their uniforms," the diplomat said, quoting the politician.
"It is a serious problem because the rebels have rejeced any mediation. They say they are ready to fight to the end and are prepared for anything," he said.

U.S. Marine task force commander Lieutenant-Colonel Tom Greenwood said the evacuation "was no problem for us." His landing team took no chances, however, deploying 200 marines on the ground with another 100 on standby on a support ship.
Marines checked the nationality of evacuees and helped women and children trailing belongings through a long queue formed by the more than 300 American passport holders leaving.

Several Europeans and nationals of other countries milled in the hotel lobby hoping to be ferried to the Kearsarge. Lieutenant-Colonel Sam Helland told CNN more than 500 people were expected to be evacuated.
Once the evacuation was completed, the ship would sail for Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea, where evacuees would make their own travel arrangements.
In London, nearly 400 Westerners arrived on Friday after being evacuated. Some spoke of fearing death after Sunday's coup as soldiers rammed through gates and then looted their houses.
Military sources said the evacuations were the main reason the Nigerians had not yet acted despite support for their role by the United States and the regional bloc, ECOWAS.
"The United States particularly insisted against any action that would traumatise women and children being evacuated," one source told Reuters.
The coup leaders have shown increasing signs of anxiety as foreign countries accelerate the evacuation of their nationals. Former colonial ruler Britain completed its airlift on Thursday.
